UX Case Study · 2020

TerraLens

Making climate and land data readable for national food-security planners.

RoleProduct Designer
ClientInternational agri-development agency
PartnerRegional geospatial research centre
Built bySoftware studio (my employer)
Mohamed Nishaz · Product Design01
At a glance

A GIS dashboard where non-specialists can explore, layer and compare agro-ecological data on one map.

The problem

Raster maps of soil, climate and crop suitability existed, but they were spread across datasets and tools built for GIS experts. Decision-makers needed to combine spatial data with their conventional datasets and answer planning questions themselves.

What I did

Owned the UX and UI for the first phase: information architecture, the explore map, the layer catalogue, scenario parameter flows, map comparison, validation and empty states, and dev handoff notes.

What changed

A loose set of layers became four guided modules and a two-map comparison tool. Questions that needed a GIS analyst became a few dropdowns, with every rule documented for developers.

4

data modules: location, land, agro-climate, suitability & yield

5

layer groups in the catalogue: base, soil, climate, hydrology, land use

2

comparison views: swipe slider and side by side

15+

interaction rules handed to engineering as on-canvas notes

TerraLens02
01 · Why this was worth solving

Good data, locked behind expert tools.

Agro-ecological zoning tells a country where each crop can grow, today and under future climate scenarios. That shapes food-security and land-use policy. But each question involves many variables:

Where?

Region, province, district, watershed or agro-ecology zone

Which crop?

Wheat, barley, buckwheat…

When?

A historic range, or a future year such as 2050 or 2080

Which scenario?

Climate pathway (RCP), CO₂ fertilization, input level

Which layer?

Soil (9), climate, hydrology, land use, base layers

Compared to what?

Another period, scenario or indicator

The design challenge: let a planner set all of that without seeing all of it at once.

TerraLens03
02 · How I decided what to focus on

Three principles from client sessions and technical limits.

01

The map is the hero

Controls sit in collapsible side panels and floating tool rails, so the map always keeps the centre of the screen. Charts summarise the current selection on the right.

02

One decision at a time

Each field appears only when it becomes relevant. For example, the climate-scenario field shows up only after a future year is chosen, and a historic period swaps the year list for a range slider.

03

Design for the API, not against it

In a client meeting we learned that hover read-outs on raster data were too costly because each one triggers API calls. So statistics open with an explicit click via the info tool, which is honest about the wait.

TerraLens04
03 · Structure

Four modules, read top to bottom.

The left panel follows the order a planner thinks in: first where, then what the land is like, then what the climate does, and finally what can grow.

1

Location / Area. Open on first load and collapses once layers are added.

2

Modules. Each one expands to a summary card with Edit and Clear.

3

Map tools. Zoom to layer, fullscreen, info, print and add-to-note, labelled on first use.

4

Insight rail. Charts for the current selection, and collapsible to give the map more room.

TerraLens05
04 · Explore

Pick an area, then pull in the layers you need.

Area by meaning, not coordinates. Choose how to slice the map first (region, province, district, watershed or agro-ecology zone). The next field's label then changes to match.

A catalogue, not a menu. Layers are grouped into tabs, each with a thumbnail and description. Add and remove are toggles, and Cancel leaves the panel untouched.

Selections stay visible. Added layers appear as cards in the panel, so users never have to guess what is on the map.

TerraLens06
05 · Iteration & feedback

Map comparison, version 1 → version 2.

Version 1
Version 2 · shipped to dev

The first version put everything up front: a global toolbar (location, crop, area type, base layer, Load) plus four empty dropdowns on each side. Users could hit Load too early and get the error “Select right AEZ layers”.

After review, users choose what to compare first, and both panels default to that indicator. Each side asks only for period, scenario and duration, with Add and Clear. The view mode moved into a single “Select preview” choice.

TerraLens07
06 · The solution

Two ways to see change: swipe it, or set it side by side.

Swipe slider. Best for spotting exactly where a boundary or value shifts between two scenarios. Each side keeps its own legend and unit.

Side by side. Best for reading two full maps. Each map has its own zoom and layer controls. The choice sits behind one “Select preview” button so the toolbar stays simple.

TerraLens08
07 · Craft in the details

Every state written down for engineering.

Map tools fail quietly when data is missing. I designed the unhappy paths and pinned each rule beside its screen in Figma.

  • Continue stays disabled until every required field is selected
  • Inline field errors name the missing input, e.g. “Please select input level”
  • “Data not available” explains the problem and asks for different values, instead of showing an empty map
  • Legends appear only when there is data: none for a location-only selection
  • Panels collapse automatically after Add or Clear, so the map comes back into view
  • Historic periods show the chosen range, e.g. “Selected date range: 2008–2009”
  • Info on click: raster statistics open in a popup, not on hover
TerraLens09
08 · Outcome & reflection

What changed, and what I’d do next time.

Outcome

  • Delivered the IA, explore and comparison flows for the platform’s first phase, ready for development
  • Turned expert-only GIS steps into guided dropdown flows for planners
  • Settled API-driven trade-offs (click vs. hover) in design, not during build

Learning 01

Ask about data cost early. One conversation about API calls changed the whole interaction model for map statistics.

Learning 02

Fewer fields up front beat “everything visible”. The second comparison version removed an entire toolbar and the errors it caused.

Next time

I’d run task-based tests with planners on the comparison flow and track how long it takes to reach a first useful map.

Thank you.
